nameStory: The Ant Woodlouse gets its name from its remarkable lifestyle choice — it's a tiny crustacean that has decided to move in with ants! Unlike other woodlice that live under logs and stones, this species has evolved to be the ultimate houseguest, living exclusively in ant colonies. It's essentially the "pet" woodlouse of the ant world, though the ants probably don't mind since it helps clean up their nest.
description: The Ant Woodlouse is a tiny, pure white crustacean that looks like a miniature pill bug or roly-poly. At just 4 millimeters long (about the size of a small ant), it has a distinctive oval, flattened body and unusually short antennae compared to other woodlice. This little creature is completely dependent on ant colonies for survival, living inside their nests and feeding on ant waste and mildew. You'll never find one living the typical woodlouse life under a rotting log — they're strictly ant apartment dwellers!

idTips.label: Pure white color
idTips.description: Completely white or pale cream colored body with no pigmentation patterns — looks almost translucent or ghostly compared to the gray-brown woodlice you typically find

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Only 4mm long, about the size of your pinky fingernail width — much smaller than common woodlice which are typically 10-20mm

idTips.label: Oval, flattened shape
idTips.description: Distinctively oval and somewhat flattened body shape, less cylindrical than typical pill bugs, with a smooth texture

idTips.label: Short antennae
idTips.description: Noticeably shorter antennae compared to other woodlice — they don't extend much beyond the head

idTips.label: Found with ants
idTips.description: Always discovered in or very near ant colonies, particularly yellow meadow ants and black garden ants — never found alone under logs or stones

habitat: Look for Ant Woodlice exclusively in and around ant nests, particularly those of yellow meadow ants (Lasius flavus) and black garden ants (Lasius niger). They're most commonly found in the soil chambers and tunnels of established ant colonies in gardens, meadows, and forest edges. Since they depend entirely on ants for shelter and food, you'll never find them in typical woodlouse habitats like under logs or stones.

seasonality.spring: Active in ant colonies as ants become more active with warming weather. Look for them when disturbing ant nests during garden work.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when ant colonies are most established and active. Most likely time to encounter them when ants are foraging heavily.
seasonality.fall: Still active in ant nests as colonies prepare for winter. May be found deeper in nest chambers as ants move underground.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active, staying deep in ant nest chambers below the frost line with their ant hosts.

funFact: These tiny woodlice are so specialized for ant life that they've completely lost their ability to live independently — they literally cannot survive without their ant roommates and have evolved to be the perfect houseguests by cleaning up ant waste!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with tiny dwarf woodlice (Trichoniscidae family), but those are usually grayish and found in typical woodlouse habitats under logs and stones, not in ant nests. Remember: white color + ant nest = Ant Woodlouse, gray color + under logs = dwarf woodlouse.
contextualKnowledge: Be careful with scientific names — there's another completely different species called Porcellio hoffmannseggii (also abbreviated P. hoffmannseggii) that's a regular woodlouse. The identical abbreviations can cause confusion in scientific literature, so always check the full genus name when researching.
compareHints: This is the only Platyarthrus species in New England, making it unique among local woodlice. Compared to other small woodlice in the region, it's distinguished by its pure white coloration, exclusive association with ant nests, and smaller size. Most similar species in the dwarf woodlouse family (Trichoniscidae) are grayish in color and live independently under rotting wood or stones, not in ant colonies.
